units.title: Unit 13 — Weather
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 30–31 (PDF pages 34–35).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Topics: Travel and the environment · weather, forecasts and storms
learningObjectives: Describe sunshine, precipitation, frost, fog and wind with natural intensity and condition collocations.
Distinguish heavy rain from strong wind, dense fog from patches of fog, and frost and wind opposites.
Explain weather changes and the effects of severe weather on places and buildings.
Recognise weather-report language and selected answer-key examples of wind, rain and snow.

items.example: After several rainy weeks, the island finally enjoyed unbroken sunshine.
items.note: Unbroken suggests continuous sunshine without cloudy intervals.

items.example: The pavement was scorching hot by midday.
items.note: Scorching is an emphatic adjective for extremely high temperatures; usually refers to weather or things exposed to heat.

items.example: On Sunday we sat outside to soak up the sunshine.
items.note: Informal and positive: enjoy exposure to sunshine, often while relaxing.

items.pt: chovendo muito; caindo uma chuva torrencial
items.example: It was pouring with rain when the concert ended.
items.note: Be pouring with rain describes very heavy rainfall; the subject is typically it.

items.example: Torrential rain flooded the streets within an hour.
items.note: Torrential intensifies rain much more strongly than heavy.

items.example: It was freezing cold at the bus stop before sunrise.
items.note: An emphatic everyday expression for extreme cold; it does not imply a temperature below zero.

items.example: We saw a break in the clouds just before sunset.
items.note: A temporary opening in cloud cover through which the sky or sun may be visible.

items.example: Thick cloud blocked the sun throughout the afternoon.
items.note: Thick cloud refers to substantial cloud cover; cloud is often uncountable in this weather sense.

items.example: The sky is turning grey; it looks like rain.
items.note: Said when the weather suggests rain is likely but may not yet have started.

items.example: It tends to rain heavily in this region during summer storms.
items.note: Heavy is the natural adjective with rain, while heavily is the corresponding adverb with the verb rain.

items.pt: o tempo piora; as condições meteorológicas se deterioram
items.example: Weather deteriorates rapidly in the mountains when storms approach.
items.note: Deteriorate is relatively formal; get worse is a more conversational alternative.

items.example: We will leave early if the weather improves overnight.
items.note: Improve is the opposite of deteriorate when discussing weather conditions.

items.example: Thick fog delayed several early-morning trains.
items.note: Thick describes fog that seriously limits visibility.

items.example: Drivers slowed down because dense fog covered the road.
items.note: Dense fog usually reduces visibility more extensively than isolated patches of fog.

items.pt: bancos de neblina; trechos com nevoeiro
items.example: There were patches of fog along the road to the valley.
items.note: Patch denotes a localised area; plural patches can alternate with clear stretches.

items.pt: bancos de névoa; trechos com neblina
items.example: Patches of mist drifted across the fields at dawn.
items.note: Mist commonly suggests thinner moisture in the air than dense fog.

items.pt: um manto de neblina; nevoeiro cobrindo uma área extensa
items.example: A blanket of fog hid the harbour from view.
items.note: A figurative, somewhat literary expression for widespread continuous fog.

items.pt: a neblina desce; o nevoeiro se forma
items.example: Fog comes down quickly near the river after dark.
items.note: Come down means that fog develops or spreads over an area; it does not mean rain begins.

items.example: The fog lifts late in the morning on most clear days.
items.note: Lift means that fog clears, allowing better visibility; opposite of fog coming down.

items.example: Wear a hat when you spend hours in the strong sun.
items.note: Strong refers to intense sunlight; it does not describe wind strength here.

items.pt: sol fraco; luz solar pouco intensa
items.example: The weak sun barely warmed the garden in winter.
items.note: Weak sun contrasts with strong sun and suggests little heat or intensity.

items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: Heavy rain made the mountain path unsafe.
items.note: Say heavy rain, not strong rain.

items.pt: chuva forte com vento; chuva batida pelo vento
items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: The cyclists struggled to see through the driving rain.
items.note: Driving rain is blown forcefully, often almost horizontally, by strong wind.

items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: Heavy snow blocked the road to the village.
items.note: Heavy combines naturally with precipitation, including rain and snow.

items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: Fresh snow covered the empty football pitch.
items.note: Fresh snow is snow that has fallen recently.

items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: Our boots made a crunching sound on the crisp snow.
items.note: Crisp snow has a hard, fresh surface, often making a crunching noise underfoot.

items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: Thick snow covered the garden walls.
items.note: Thick focuses on the depth or density of accumulated snow.

items.pt: neve soprada com força pelo vento
items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: Visibility dropped sharply in the driving snow.
items.note: Driving describes snow blown hard by wind, especially during a storm.

items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: A hard frost damaged the garden plants overnight.
items.note: Hard frost is severe; the usual opposite is light frost, not soft frost.

items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: There was a light frost on the grass at sunrise.
items.note: Use light rather than soft to describe a mild frost.

items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: A strong wind shook the windows all night.
items.note: Strong is normal for wind, unlike rain, which takes heavy.

items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: A light wind cooled the terrace in the afternoon.
items.note: Light is a natural opposite of strong when describing wind.

items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: High winds forced the ferry service to stop.
items.note: Typically plural; especially common in weather forecasts and warnings.

items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: A biting wind blew across the empty platform.
items.note: Biting implies unpleasant cold rather than simply strong wind.

items.pt: o vento aumenta; o vento ganha força
items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: The wind picks up after sunset near the coast.
items.note: Pick up means grow stronger; the opposite here is die down.

items.pt: o vento diminui; o vento perde força
items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: The wind dies down before dawn in this valley.
items.note: Die down means gradually become weaker or less intense.

items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: A cold wind blows through the narrow streets in winter.
items.note: Blow is the conventional verb for wind; choose a modifier such as strongly for intensity.

items.pt: o vento assobia; o vento uiva
items.section: B · Rain, snow, frost and wind
items.example: The wind whistles through gaps in the old windows.
items.note: Whistle describes a high-pitched sound produced as wind passes an opening.

items.section: C · Extreme weather and its consequences
items.example: Freak storms damaged several coastal villages in early spring.
items.note: Freak marks weather as extremely unusual or unexpected for the place or season.

items.section: C · Extreme weather and its consequences
items.example: Freak weather conditions interrupted the outdoor festival.
items.note: Journalistic phrase stressing abnormal weather; freak is not simply a synonym for bad.

items.section: C · Extreme weather and its consequences
items.example: Gale-force winds prevented the fishing boats from leaving port.
items.note: A forecast and news expression for exceptionally strong winds; gale-force is a compound modifier.

items.pt: um rio transborda; um rio sai do leito
items.section: C · Extreme weather and its consequences
items.example: If a river bursts its banks, nearby roads can flood.
items.note: Burst its banks means water rises beyond the river channel; plural rivers take their banks.

items.pt: causar danos a propriedades; causar danos materiais
items.section: C · Extreme weather and its consequences
items.example: The hailstorm could cause damage to property across the district.
items.note: Property refers to buildings or possessions; damage is normally uncountable in this sense.

items.section: C · Extreme weather and its consequences
items.example: Several farm buildings were destroyed by the sudden storm.
items.note: Destroy implies much more severe harm than damage.

items.section: C · Extreme weather and its consequences
items.example: Two roofs were torn off during the windstorm.
items.note: Tear off describes removing something violently, especially through strong wind.

items.section: C · Extreme weather and its consequences
items.example: Several fences were blown down near the railway line.
items.note: Blow down describes wind forcing an upright object to fall.

items.section: C · Extreme weather and its consequences
items.example: Severe weather conditions delayed the mountain rescue.
items.note: Severe is common in formal warnings and forecasts about dangerous weather.

items.section: C · Extreme weather and its consequences
items.example: A powerful cyclone could devastate a town without adequate defences.
items.note: Devastate denotes extensive destruction; stronger than simply damage.

items.pt: nem uma brisa; ausência completa de vento
items.example: There was not a breath of wind on the lake at dawn.
items.note: Fixed expression for completely still air.

items.example: A gust of wind knocked my hat into the water.
items.note: A gust is a sudden short increase in wind speed.

items.example: We decided to walk despite the light rain.
items.note: Light describes mild rain; compare heavy rain.

items.example: We got caught in a downpour of rain on the way home.
items.note: Downpour is a sudden period of extremely heavy rainfall.

items.example: We had a shower of rain just after lunchtime.
items.note: A shower is often shorter and more localised than persistent rain.

items.example: Snow falls regularly in the hills each winter.
items.note: Fall is the usual verb for snow coming down from the sky.

items.example: Snow melts quickly on these south-facing slopes.
items.note: Melt describes solid snow changing into water as the temperature rises.

items.example: A blanket of snow covered the rooftops overnight.
items.note: A figurative expression for broad, fairly continuous coverage.

sectionsChecked: A · Weather postcards and everyday conditions
B · Weather conditions: fog, sunshine, rain, snow, frost and wind

units.title: Unit 14 — Travel
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 32–33 (PDF pages 36–37).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Topics: Travel and the environment · journeys, flights and accommodation
learningObjectives: Use travel for the general activity, trip for a particular visit and journey for the process or route.
Choose appropriate collocations for air travel, seating, connections, procedures and flight conditions.
Describe hotels, prices and reservations with natural accommodation phrases.
Apply contrasts including outward/return journey, domestic/international flight and smooth/bumpy flight.

items.pt: organizar uma viagem; providenciar os preparativos de viagem
items.example: We need to make travel arrangements before the conference registration closes.
items.note: Travel arrangements include transport, timing and sometimes accommodation; travel is uncountable in this use.

items.example: A travel agent helped us choose flights within our budget.
items.note: A person or business arranging travel; travel modifies agent without a plural s.

items.example: Our company has reduced its spending on business travel.
items.note: Refers to work-related travelling in general, not one specific journey.

items.pt: viagem a trabalho; viagem de negócios
items.example: The sales director made a business trip to Lisbon last month.
items.note: A trip is one identifiable visit or journey; contrast with business travel in general.

items.example: The overnight bus ride was a tiring journey for the whole family.
items.note: Journey emphasises the experience or process of travelling from one place to another.

items.pt: viagem de volta; trajeto de retorno
items.example: The return journey took longer because of traffic.
items.note: Return refers to travel back; contrast with the outward journey.

items.example: We stopped twice during the outward journey to the coast.
items.note: Outward is the journey away from the starting point, opposite of return journey.

items.example: Have a safe journey and send us a message when you arrive.
items.note: Often used as a parting wish; safe travels is another common expression.

items.example: We picked up some travel brochures at the tourism fair.
items.note: Travel brochures provide destination and holiday information.

items.example: Our family plans two camping trips each summer.
items.note: Trip is countable and refers to separate outings or journeys.

items.example: An overnight journey by train can save you a hotel stay.
items.note: Overnight indicates that travelling continues through the night.

items.example: We organised a day trip to a coastal town.
items.note: A day trip starts and ends within the same day, without an overnight stay.

items.example: They booked a boat trip around the bay.
items.note: Trip focuses on the outing or excursion; boat identifies the means of travel.

items.pt: fazer um passeio de um dia; fazer um bate-volta
items.example: You could take a day trip to the castle while staying in the city.
items.note: Take is natural with trip when describing an excursion.

items.example: We hope to take a boat trip along the river tomorrow.
items.note: A natural verb–noun combination for a recreational journey by boat.

items.pt: passear para conhecer os pontos turísticos
items.example: I would like to do some sightseeing after the training course.
items.note: Do sightseeing refers to visiting sights as an activity, rather than taking one specific trip.

items.example: The airline offers in-flight entertainment on longer routes.
items.note: In-flight means during a flight; refers to films, music or other passenger media.

items.example: I read the in-flight magazine before the meal service began.
items.note: A publication supplied to passengers on an aircraft.

items.example: We expect to land at the airport before midnight.
items.note: Land at is used with an airport; land in is possible with a city or country.

items.example: Please fasten your seatbelt before the aircraft moves.
items.note: A formal safety instruction; fasten means secure something with its fastening.

items.example: Passengers can board the plane through the rear door today.
items.note: Board means get onto an aircraft, train or ship, common in travel announcements.

items.example: The aircraft is due to take off at half past six.
items.note: Take off is the usual phrasal verb for an aircraft leaving the ground.

items.example: We might miss a connecting flight if the first plane is delayed.
items.note: A connecting flight is the next flight in a multi-leg route; miss means fail to catch it.

items.example: For a domestic flight, check the airline’s baggage rules.
items.note: A domestic flight operates within one country, unlike an international flight.

items.example: An international flight usually requires additional travel documents.
items.note: A flight between countries, in contrast to a domestic flight.

items.example: I chose a window seat so I could see the mountains.
items.note: A seat beside the aircraft window, contrasting with an aisle seat.

items.example: An aisle seat gives me more freedom to stand up.
items.note: Aisle is pronounced with a silent s; this seat is next to the passage through the cabin.

items.example: They booked a charter flight for the group holiday.
items.note: A charter flight is hired for a particular service or group, contrasting with scheduled flights.

items.example: We chose a scheduled flight with an established airline.
items.note: A scheduled flight operates according to an airline’s regular timetable.

items.pt: um voo tranquilo; um voo sem turbulência
items.example: We had a smooth flight despite the gloomy weather.
items.note: Smooth describes comfortable flight conditions with little turbulence.

items.example: The pilot warned us that it might be a bumpy flight.
items.note: Bumpy is the opposite of smooth for flight conditions.

items.example: We stayed at a family-run hotel near the historic centre.
items.note: Family-run refers to who manages the hotel, not necessarily who stays there.

items.example: The photos looked attractive, but it turned out to be a run-down hotel.
items.note: Run-down means neglected or in poor condition; it is not related to low prices alone.

items.example: They celebrated their anniversary at a luxury hotel.
items.note: Luxury is a noun used as a modifier, meaning very high comfort or standard.

items.example: The visiting executives booked rooms at a smart hotel near the station.
items.note: Smart can mean stylish or upmarket in British English, not technologically connected.

items.example: Students often look for budget accommodation near the university.
items.note: Budget is used before accommodation to indicate a lower-cost option.

items.example: Please make a reservation before arriving during the holiday weekend.
items.note: Make, not do, combines with reservation; in British English booking is also common.

items.example: Every guesthouse in the town was fully booked for the festival.
items.note: Means all available places or rooms are reserved; not merely busy.

items.example: Our flight changed direction en route to Madrid.
items.note: A somewhat formal expression meaning while travelling towards a destination.

items.example: The flight is delayed because of thick fog at the destination airport.
items.note: A flight may be delayed before departure or in its arrival schedule.

B · Flights: airline announcements and passenger terms
